Silver Ring Value Partners Limited Partnership • One Boston Place, Suite 2600, Boston, MA 02108 • www.silverringvaluepartners.com 
February 6th, 2026 
 
 
Dear Partners: 
 
I hope that you are doing well. The Partnership had an excellent year, with net returns of 106% in 
2025. More importantly, the hard work of improving the process over the last few years has 
resulted in better decision making and a better-balanced portfolio. 
 
You can learn a lot about an investor when they go through a period of poor performance. Some 
quit. Others abandon their process and swing for the fences to try and recover or perhaps go to the 
other extreme and lose confidence in themselves and shy away from taking any risk, no matter how 
attractive. 
 
I am proud that I did none of those things but instead used it as motivation to improve myself as an 
investor and to work harder. I am still far from perfect, and there is always room for improvement. 
As much as the challenges over the prior years were trying, I believe the partnership is now in a 
much better place on the other side. 
 
Speaking of improving as an investor, I launched a project that I am really excited about that aims 
to help me and others do just that. In my 25+ years as a professional investor I have come to 
realize that there is a big gap for systematic improvement in a time-efficient way for experienced 
investors. 
 
What I am launching is a platform built around a weekly case study, the 10-Minute Investment 
Autops

Warner Bros.: How 5 Mental Models Turned Lonely Conviction into a 
Big Win 
 
Since Warner Bros. (WBD) was such a major contributor to results in 2025, I wanted to spend some 
time on it to illustrate the process. However, first I want to make two points: 
 
1. Despite the magnitude of the contribution to returns from WBD, the position was structured 
such that we could never have lost more than 5% of the portfolio, consistent with my risk 
management parameters. 
2. If we were to remove all gains from WBD, the portfolio would still have been up over 30% in 
2025. 
 
It felt lonely owning Warner Bros. 
 
My former colleagues were telling me I might be wrong. An investor friend, whom I highly respect, 
had sold his shares. A hedge-fund media specialist didn’t want to touch it with a 10-foot pole. 
 
The few people I knew who still owned Warner Bros. had only a small position. 
 
Yet, I was getting increasingly excited. Charlie Munger once described a lollapalooza effect as one 
where multiple mental models converge – and I strongly felt that was the case here. Below are the 
five mental models I used that allowed me to build conviction to make the investment a large 
position and reap a huge profit for the Partnership. 
 
1. Good Business / Bad Business Combination

Portfolio Metrics 
I track a number of metrics for the portfolio to help me better understand it and manage risk. I track 
these both at a given point in time, and as a time series to analyze how the portfolio has changed 
over time to make sure that it is invested in the way that I intend for it to be. Below I share a 
number of these metrics, what each means, and what it can tell us about the portfolio. As time 
passes, you should be able to refer to these charts and graphs to help you gain deeper insight into 
how I am applying my process. 
 
Price % Base Case Value 
This metric tracks the portfolio’s weighted average ratio between market price and my Base Case 
intrinsic value estimate of each security. This ratio is presented both including cash and 
equivalents, which are valued at a Price to Value of 100%, and excluding those. All else being 
equal, the lower these numbers are, the better. Excluding cash and equivalents, a level above 
100% would be a red flag, indicating that the portfolio is trading above my estimate of intrinsic 
value. Levels between 90% and 100% I would characterize as a yellow flag, suggesting that the 
portfolio is very close to my estimate of value. Levels between 75% and 90% are lukewarm, while 
levels below 75% are attractive.

Normalized Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio 
I supplement my intrinsic value estimates, which are based on Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) 
analysis, with a number of other metrics that I use to make sure that my value estimates make 
sense. One of the more useful ones is the Normalized P/E ratio. The denominator is my estimate of 
earnings over the next 12 months, adjusted for any one-time/unsustainable factors, and if 
necessary adjusted for the cyclical nature of the business to reflect a mid-cycle economic 
environment. The numerator is adjusted for any excess assets (e.g. excess cash) not used to 
generate my estimate of normalized earnings. One way to interpret this number is that its inverse 
represents the rate of return we would receive on our purchase price if earnings remained 
permanently flat. So a normalized P/E of 10x would be consistent with an expectation of a 10% 
return. While the future is uncertain, it is typically my goal to invest in businesses whose value is 
increasing over time. If I am correct in my analysis, our return should exceed the inverse of the 
normalized P/E ratio over a long period of time. The graph below represents the weighted average 
normalized P/E for the equities in the portfolio.
